newsitem.title: CHINA: China sees 1997 wheat imports sharply falling.
newsitem.headline: China sees 1997 wheat imports sharply falling.

text.p: China's wheat imports are expected to fall sharply in 1997 compared with last year because of bumper domestic harvests, officials said on Monday.

"Judging from the market situation, wheat imports this year will be significantly lower than last year," said an official of the China National Cereals, Oils and Foodstuffs Import and Export Corp (COFCO).
The official declined to give a projection for import levels this year.
The official Futures Herald newspaper has projected China's net imports of wheat at 6.0-10 million tonnes in 1997.
China imported 550,000 tonnes of wheat in the first four months of the year, down 72.5 percent compared with the year-ago period, customs figures showed.
China imported a total of 8.25 million tonnes of wheat in 1996, down 28.8 percent compared with the previous year, customs figures showed.

"The decline is mainly a result of market forces rather than instructions from the government," the COFCO official said by telephone. Demand for imported wheat has fallen because of at least two consecutive bumper harvests.
China's 1997 wheat output was expected to hit about 115 million tonnes, exceeding demand that is projected at 113.2 million tonnes, official media has said.
China produced 109 million tonnes of wheat in 1996, the China Grains, Oils and Feed Information newsletter quoted the Ministry of Agriculture as saying.
China still needs imports of high-quality wheat from Canada, the United States and elsewhere to produce fine flour for the food industry, an official of the State Grain Reserves Administration said.
"We still need wheat imports to make up for some shortfalls," he said. Rising living standards have pushed up consumption of high-protein food.
China's own production of high-quality wheat was limited and could not keep up with rising consumption, he said, but declined to give further details.
